snip.s: Heart failure: which tests and why

snip.t: Venous return pathways (jugular veins, superior/inferior vena cava, hepatic veins): Elevated right‑atrial pressure transmits back to the jugular veins (raised JVP) and hepatic veins (congestive hepatomegaly).
snip.s: Approach to Cardiovascular Symptoms and Examination

snip.t: Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Elevated JVP indicates increased right atrial pressure, common in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Elevated, often with a prominent 'a' wave (right atrial contraction against a stiff RV) and sometimes a prominent 'v' wave (tricuspid regurgitation).
Haemodynamics from RHC: Higher mPAP, higher PVR, lower cardiac index, higher right atrial pressure indicate more severe disease.
Right atrial and ventricular diastolic pressures rise first due to their lower filling pressures, leading to the characteristic haemodynamic compromise.
| Echocardiography | Effusion volume and hemodynamic compromise | Anechoic fluid rim; right atrial systolic collapse and right ventricular diastolic collapse signal tamponade |
Elevated Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Reflects high right atrial pressure secondary to elevated right ventricular end-diastolic pressure or biventricular failure.
